 These Veterans Day facts from History.com trace the holiday from Armistice Day to today, covering its date changes, its meaning and the veterans it honors
 1 / 12 List slides Veterans Day facts most Americans don't know, according to History.com List slides Previous Start over By Cris Tolomia · Updated October 27, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 November 11 has not always been called Veterans Day, and the holiday has not always fallen on November 11. It began under a different name after World War I. It was later renamed, moved to a Monday in October and then returned to its original date.
 History.com has gathered a set of Veterans Day facts that follow that path from 1919 forward. The 10 slides below are a selection drawn from that material. They are not its complete list, and they are not a ranking. Each slide covers one subject and can be read on its own.
 The first four slides deal with the calendar. They trace the holiday's start as Armistice Day and the moment in 1918 behind its date. They also cover the 1954 change of name and a period when the holiday moved to October.
 The next two slides cover meaning and ritual. One explains how History.com distinguishes Veterans Day from Memorial Day. The other looks at the annual memorial service held at Arlington National Cemetery.
 The last four slides turn to veterans themselves. One looks at candidates in the 2022 midterm elections who claimed military experience. Another covers women veterans and the Vietnam, Gulf War and Korean War eras. The final two address how many World War II veterans were still living as of 2025 and which states had the highest share of veterans as of 2023.
 The 10 facts track how one moment in November 1918 led to a holiday that honors service in war and in peacetime.
 Veterans Day began as Armistice Day in 1919 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Veterans Day started out as Armistice Day, first observed on November 11, 1919. That first observance came one year after World War I ended, according to History.com .
 The original name pointed back to the armistice that closed that war. The holiday did not reach its permanent status in one step.
 Formal recognition came in stages. In 1926, Congress passed a resolution calling for an annual observance, History.com reports.
 That resolution set the expectation of a yearly observance. It did not yet make November 11 a national holiday.
 That status came next. Starting in 1938, November 11 became a national holiday, according to History.com.
 Three dates mark the path from a first observance to a fixed place on the national calendar: 1919, 1926 and 1938.
 Why Veterans Day is held on November 11 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Veterans Day falls on November 11 because of one moment in 1918. History.com ties the date to the "eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month" of that year, the moment that marked the end of World War I.
 The quoted phrase is History.com's own wording. It fixes the end of the war to a specific hour on a specific day, not just to a year or a season.
 The phrase counts the month, the day and the hour with the same number. In calendar terms, the eleventh month is November and the eleventh day is the 11th. That pairing is the date the holiday carries.
 The hour in the phrase does not appear in the date itself. The holiday keeps the month and the day from that moment in 1918.
 Eisenhower renamed Armistice Day as Veterans Day in 1954 
 Illustration: Quartz
 President Dwight D. Eisenhower formally renamed the holiday in 1954, according to History.com. The observance Americans had known as Armistice Day has carried the name Veterans Day ever since.
 The old name referred to the armistice that ended World War I. The new name refers instead to the people who served in the military.
 The renaming changed what the holiday was called, not when it was held. In 1954, the observance still fell on November 11.
 How the Uniform Holidays Bill moved Veterans Day to October 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Veterans Day once fell on a Monday in October instead of November 11. Congress passed the Uniform Holidays Bill in 1968, and the law shifted the holiday to the fourth Monday in October, according to History.com.
 The move tied Veterans Day to a weekday rather than a fixed calendar date. A fourth Monday lands on a different date from one year to the next. Under the new schedule, the holiday would always fall on a Monday.
 The change did not take effect right away. Congress acted in 1968, but the October date did not go into effect until 1971.
 The October schedule did not last. In 1975, President Gerald Ford $F returned Veterans Day to November 11.
 History.com reports that Ford pointed to the historical significance of the November 11 date in making that decision.
 Veterans Day is observed on November 11 today, the same date it held before the Uniform Holidays Bill moved it.
 How Veterans Day differs from Memorial Day 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Veterans Day honors all American veterans, living or dead, and it covers veterans of every war, according to History.com. The holiday gives special weight to thanking living veterans who served honorably.
 History.com draws its contrast between Veterans Day and Memorial Day around that scope. The difference it describes rests on who the day is meant to recognize.
 Living veterans sit at the center of that distinction. Veterans Day directs its thanks to people who completed their service and are still alive to receive it. Veterans who have died remain within its purpose as well.
 Service during a war is not a requirement. History.com specifies that the thanks extend to those who served honorably in wartime or in peacetime. A veteran whose time in uniform fell between conflicts is honored on the same terms as one who served during a war.
 No single conflict defines the holiday. Its reach takes in veterans of all wars, rather than one era or one generation of service members.
 History.com also qualifies the kind of service the day recognizes. The thanks go to those who served honorably, whether that service came in combat or in peacetime.
 Arlington National Cemetery's Veterans Day memorial service 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Arlington National Cemetery holds a memorial service every year on Veterans Day, according to History.com. It also holds a separate annual memorial service on Memorial Day.
 The cemetery observes both holidays, and each one gets its own service.
 More than 400,000 people are buried at Arlington, History.com reports. Most of them served in the military. That wording means not everyone buried there was a service member.
 Military veterans who ran for office in the 2022 midterms 
 Illustration: Quartz
 About one in five candidates for U.S. Senate, U.S. House or governor in the 2022 midterm elections claimed some degree of military experience, according to History.com. Expressed as a percentage, the share is 21 percent.
 The figure covers three kinds of races. Two are federal: contests for the Senate and for the House of Representatives. The third is statewide and covers campaigns for governor. The figure does not extend to other offices on the 2022 ballot.
 The count rests on what candidates said about their own backgrounds. The word "claimed" marks the number as a tally of candidates' own descriptions. History.com does not say whether those descriptions were checked against service records.
 "Some degree of military experience" is also a broad phrase. It could cover a wide range of service histories. History.com does not break the figure down by branch, length of service, rank or deployment.
 The 21 percent describes people who ran, not people who won. The figure does not show how many of those candidates took office after the election. It also does not measure how many veterans hold seats in Congress or serve as governors.
 History.com does not compare the 2022 share with earlier election cycles. The number captures one midterm year rather than a trend. It appears among the site's Veterans Day facts as a measure of how often military service featured in the backgrounds of people seeking high office.
 Women veterans and the Vietnam, Gulf War and Korean War eras 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Women make up more than 11 percent of living U.S. veterans, according to History.com. The same fact page also groups living veterans by the era in which they served.
 The share for women applies only to living veterans. It does not describe everyone who has ever served in the U.S. military.
 History.com does not break that share down by era. The page gives no count of women for the Vietnam War era, the Gulf War era or the Korean War.
 Among the three eras covered here, the Gulf War era holds the largest group, with 7.8 million living veterans. History.com gives no start or end date for that era.
 The Vietnam War era follows, with 5.6 million living veterans. History.com dates that era from 1950 to 1973.
 The Korean War accounts for 767,000 living veterans. That is the smallest of the three counts on the page.
 These numbers count survivors, not service. A tally of living veterans shows how many people from a given period are still alive. It does not measure how many people served during that period.
 That distinction shapes how the order of the three groups should be read. A larger living count for one era does not show that more people served in it. It shows only that more of its veterans are alive.
 The page does not attach a reporting year to the share of women or to any of the three era counts. It also gives no total for the living veteran population. Without that total, the era counts cannot be read as shares of a whole.
 How many World War II veterans are still living 
 Illustration: Quartz
 About 45,418 American veterans of World War II were still living as of 2025, according to History.com. Around 16 million Americans served in the war.
 The two figures measure different groups. The larger one counts everyone who served in World War II. The smaller one counts only the members of that group who were still alive in 2025.
 Side by side, the numbers show how much the group has shrunk. The service total is measured in millions. The living count is measured in tens of thousands.
 Only a small fraction of the Americans who served in the war were still alive by 2025.
 The two figures differ in precision. History.com ties the living count to a specific year, 2025. It gives the service total as an approximation rather than an exact number.
 Alaska, Virginia and Montana had the highest share of veterans in 2023 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Alaska, Virginia and Montana were the three U.S. states with the highest share of veterans as of 2023, according to History.com.
 The ranking measures a proportion, not a headcount. A state places high when veterans make up a large part of its residents. It does not need to have the most veterans in total.
 History.com names the three states as a group. It gives no percentage for any of them and does not say which of the three ranks first.
 That limits what the list can show. Without percentages, the gap among the three states cannot be measured. Neither can the distance between them and the rest of the country.
 The ranking is also tied to a single year. History.com dates it to 2023. It describes the three states at that point, not across other years.
